The divergence in AI output weirdly may be the highest it’s ever been, even though adoption is the broadest it’s ever been. 

A few years ago the best productivity gains you could get, even in the most capability-aligned field (like coding), was maybe 30-50% better productivity if you were very good at it. You’d spend a decent chunk of time cleaning up the mistakes of models, the context windows were too limited to do any long running work, and the interfaces required highly synchronous interactions. 

Now, the models can do far longer tasks at a time with limited human interaction. The harnesses support agentic work that can take on these larger tasks. The models are trained on vastly better datasets for a growing array of domains so you have to intervene far less. And we have systems that better support working with many agents at once. 

In just a two year timespan, the upper limits on productivity gains have gone from 30-50% to now likely 5-10X depending on the field. So we’ve gone from an environment where living at the frontier vs. not paying attention at all could be an order of magnitude difference in your output.

This distance is only getting wider from here given the rate of progress we’re likely to see with RSI. Crazy times.

Exciting news from Agent Arena: Hy4 by @TencentHunyuan just landed #14 overall. Currently proprietary, but once its weights are released it will tie with Kimi K3.1 Pro for #1 among open models!

Across +8.5K real-world, long-horizon agentic sessions from our global community of users, Hy4 delivers +4.7% net improvement and joins the Agent Arena Pareto frontier. At $0.55/task, Hy4 costs about 62% less than Kimi K3.1 Pro (Max) at $1.46/task, and the two models’ scores are within 1 percentage point.

This release is a +3.6 percentage pt improvement from Hy4 preview at #25 with +1.1%. In fact, Hy4 improved across all key signals:
- Confirmed Success (explicit “yes, that worked” from users): #11 with +8.7% (up from #16 with +4.9%)
- Praise vs Complaint (sentiment in user reactions): #18 with +3.8% (up from #24 with +1%)
- Steerability (responding to user corrections): #14 with +5.7% (up from #27 with +0.21%)
- Bash Reliability (successful shell commands): #20 with +6.2% (up from #41 with -3.1%)

Congrats to the @TencentHunyuan team on this release!

Models by @GoogleDeepMind scale better on cost than their rivals.

Gemini 4 Carbon is the prime example. As tasks get more demanding, every rival gets more expensive relative to Carbon.

For a typical task, GPT-6 Astra by @OpenAI costs 3.4× as much, Claude Opus 5.5 by @AnthropicAI costs 3.9× as much, and GPT-6.1 Sol is the cheaper option at about half of Carbon’s cost (0.54×).

Across the 5% most expensive sessions, Carbon’s position improves against all three. Opus edges up to 4.2×, Astra’s cost roughly doubles relative to Carbon, and Sol’s discount shrinks.

This in turn can translate into meaningful savings across real-world tasks such as building an Android security app, one of many long-horizon tasks that our Agent Arena users delegate to their agents.

As tasks get more complex, @GoogleDeepMind and @XiaomiMiMo are the biggest winners in the Agent Arena.

On cheaper tasks, @OpenAI and @AnthropicAI hold 10 of the 11 frontier spots. On the most expensive 5% of sessions, they hold just 7. The freed spots go to Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6 Flash and Pro.

These shifts matter as sessions costing $100 or more are not uncommon across real-world use cases coming from Agent Arena. Even within the last 2 weeks, more than 1,000 sessions crossed that boundary, and choosing a suboptimal model might have had a meaningful impact on that final bill.

In the last 14 days, nearly 30,000 tasks ran for over an hour on Agent Arena. Within that hour, the average model made 332 tool calls.

In these long-horizon tasks, the right model choice can cut the cost by up to 66%.

In Agent Arena, an hour of work costs a median $10.51 per task with Gemini 4 Carbon, $21.13 with Claude Opus 5.5 by @AnthropicAI and $31.08 with GPT-6 Astra by @OpenAI. 

That makes Gemini 4 Carbon by @GoogleDeepmind 50% cheaper than Opus and 66% cheaper than Astra for an hour-long task.

For long-running jobs, weighing cost against capability becomes critical: Claude Opus 5.5 still scores higher, but costs twice as much per hour of work.

We’ve updated the six Artificial Analysis Capability Indexes to v2.0, aligning them with evaluations from the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0 and placing greater emphasis on Non-Hallucination and Agentic Tool Use

The Capability Indexes map tasks from O*NET occupations to benchmarks that represent them, weighting each benchmark by how often its capability appears in that occupation. There are six indexes: Finance & Accounting, Strategy & Ops, Legal, Healthcare & Medical, Engineering, and Economics.

Key changes:

➤ Finance & Accounting: increased weight on Non-Hallucination, upgraded HLE to HLE-Diamond and AA-Omniscience to v1.1, removed GDPval-AA from Agentic Knowledge Work, and removed AA-LCR from Long-Context

➤ Strategy & Ops: increased weight on Agentic Tool Use, added Non-Hallucination and upgraded AA-Omniscience to v1.1, removed GDPval-AA from Agentic Knowledge Work, and removed AA-LCR from Long-Context

➤ Legal: increased weight on Non-Hallucination, upgraded HLE to HLE-Diamond and AA-Omniscience to v1.1, removed GDPval-AA from Agentic Knowledge Work, and removed AA-LCR from Long-Context

➤ Healthcare & Medical: increased weight on Agentic Tool Use, upgraded HLE to HLE-Diamond and AA-Omniscience to v1.1, and removed GDPval-AA from Agentic Knowledge Work

➤ Engineering: added Science as a new capability sourced from CritPt v2 (Hard Subset) and Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, added FrontierCode 2.0 to Agentic Coding, upgraded HLE to HLE-Diamond and AA-Omniscience to v1.1, and removed GDPval-AA from Agentic Knowledge Work

➤ Economics: increased weights on Agentic Knowledge Work and Long-Context Reasoning, replaced AA-LCR with GDP.pdf in Long-Context Reasoning, upgraded HLE to HLE-Diamond and AA-Omniscience to v1.1, and removed GDPval-AA from Agentic Knowledge Work

Key results:

➤ Claude Opus 5.5 (max) leads in all six indexes, followed by GPT-6 Astra (max) in Finance & Accounting, Legal, and Engineering

➤ Among open weights models, Kimi K3.1 Pro (weights not yet released) leads all six indexes, at #5 to #8. MiniMax-M3.1-Flash leads in Strategy & Ops (#10), and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max) leads Healthcare & Medical (#12)

Announcing the next version of Artificial Analysis API Performance Benchmarking: Time per Task is now our headline performance metric, measuring how long a model takes to complete a task rather than how fast it streams

The update applies to the ~1,000 serverless endpoints we benchmark multiple times a day for speed, latency and caching.

Key changes:
➤ Time per Task is now the headline metric to compare models: as workloads become more agentic, the time to complete a task matters more than speed per token. A model that is fast per token but verbose can take longer than a slower model that uses fewer tokens. Time per Task divides a model's output tokens per Intelligence Index task by its End-to-End Output Speed.

➤ End-to-End Output Speed covers the full request: speed is now measured from sending the request to receiving the final token. That includes the wait before the first token (prefill, and reasoning for models that hide it) as well as generation. Output tokens now come from each provider's API-reported counts instead of the o200k_base tokenizer, and we monitor for discrepancies in reported counts.

➤ Agentic workloads are now part of every measurement: we benchmark short, document-length and long-context prompts, plus multi-turn sessions across coding and knowledge work. Headline figures are the average across these workloads over the past 5 days.

➤ API default effort is now tracked alongside highest effort: most developers run models at the effort level each lab sets as its API default, so we now benchmark key models at that setting as well as at their highest effort. Effort names are not comparable across labs, so we use each lab's own default rather than one shared setting.

Key takeaways:
➤ OpenAI models make up most of the Intelligence vs. Time per Task Pareto frontier despite slower output speeds: across effort levels, GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol hold the frontier from ~45 to ~55 on the Intelligence Index. At max effort, GPT-6 Astra runs at 51 tokens/s but finishes a task in ~17 minutes, against ~26 for Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 111 tokens/s) and ~29 minutes for Gemini 4 Carbon (high, 71 tokens/s), because it uses ~50k output tokens per task against ~120k to ~170k.

➤ API default effort cuts Time per Task by ~3 to 5x and Cost per Task by ~2 to 4x for GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5: all three default to medium effort, which scores ~5 to 11 points lower on the Intelligence Index in exchange. Claude Opus 5.5 falls from ~26 minutes and $10.04 per task at max to ~6.8 minutes and $2.45 at medium effort.

➤ Endpoints that optimize for decode speed alone see the largest drop in End-to-End Output Speed: high decode speeds can come at the cost of latency, for example by queuing requests to run at lower batch sizes, or by holding output and sending it in a single burst. Both lengthen the wait before the first token, which End-to-End Output Speed now counts.

Today, the default is trusting Claude's judgment to auto-approve. Claude does large migrations and builds new products. 

Helping build Claude Code into an industry-defining product has been the journey of a lifetime. 

Thank you to the incredible team behind Claude Code, Cowork, and Tag. These products are the sum of thousands of great ideas from you. I'll miss working with you all.

Thank you to our users for embracing a new way of working. Your constant feedback shaped so much of what we shipped and your stories made the work so meaningful.

tweets.text: Without commenting on the Takehi et al. “Weight-Space Programming” work in particular, I do suspect that a lot of RSI (and a lot of AI-driven scientific progress more broadly) will be driven by applying what were once mundane-but-difficult techniques at a scale that would have been unimaginable when the techniques were invented.

working with AI is fundamentally asking someone else to produce the work you want

we spend a lot of time communicating context, goals, giving feedback, setting rewards, shaping workflows and SOPs. it’s a managerial experience

i’ve always felt a bit sad about that, because it took away the experience and joy of being a pure craftsman that produces great work directly

chopin can’t be chopin by hiring a team and telling his employees to compose for him. these masterpieces had to be created by a craftsman directly, and i think many of us humans deep down seek that mastery and joy

when the world gets filled with more and more agents and robots, every human’s job becomes an agent manager

are we sure that’s what we want?

my open source projects collectively crossed 30k+ stars on github, going from almost zero just a few months ago! 🎉

reflecting on the journey, here are some learnings about growing and maintaining open source projects:

1. make videos sharing your OSS projects

videos, not tweets. this is probably my most important tip

i had a few viral tweets introducing my OSS projects that got lucky and had hundreds of thousands of views, but what brought in way more serious users and contributors was my youtube videos

good videos take a lot more effort to make, but it gives people a much more direct understanding of how your project works and how it delivers value. my hero project firstmate https://t.co/jtjlzK8Mdq grew largely due to my video content

make some videos. and make some more

2. use open source as a super power

i can't overstate how much better the tools got because of open source contributions from others. people bring great ideas, and test + fix the product in all kinds of edge cases that i can't possibly discover

in a way, an OSS product can guide itself towards PMF, because the community would collectively steer it towards the right direction

now that even non-developers can participate in contributing to OSS, this super power is becoming even stronger

3. set a minimum bar on contribution quality

the super power can also be a double edged sword here. especially with AI which allowed a lot more people to contribute but also lowered the bar. if left unchecked, you get a lot of noise

some projects outright disabled all PRs, while some others refuse to take anything done with AI. neither of which is the right approach IMO

my solution has been to raise the minimum bar by requiring all contributions to be raised through no-mistakes. it enforces a level of rigor, and slightly increases the cost to contribute so low quality noise would often shy away

i have a github action for enforcing this - https://t.co/LfrSUe3EuU which you can use for your projects too

4. automate as much maintenance as possible

if you've contributed to my repos, you might have seen some of my automation at work. here's an example - https://t.co/LgaqcLMRAr 

i receive dozens, sometimes hundreds of incoming issues + PRs every day across my repos - i can't imagine how i could have kept all these projects moving if i hadn't leveraged agents to automate the triage work

i run the automation in grok bot with my firstmate bot there https://t.co/KC0bhgoPMi - it can set up a different bot per each repo, and creates the routines to triage incoming issues and PRs using cursor cloud agents according to my rules, yet allows me to talk to just the firstmate about everything

an important pre-requisite to doing that is a good documented vision for your project, which i write using https://t.co/pZBFxHgJ5a - with a clearly written vision statement, your triage agents can automatically rule out changes that don't align, and focus on the ones that would further the project towards the direction you want
